name: Chocolate
toxicCompounds: Theobromine and caffeine
safeServingSize: None. Baking chocolate and cocoa powder are more dangerous than milk chocolate because they contain more theobromine.
clinicalSymptoms: Restlessness and a fast heart rate
emergencyAction: Call a poison hotline or emergency clinic with the chocolate type, the amount missing, the dog's weight, and the time eaten.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove leftovers and wrappers. Do not induce vomiting, and do not give milk, oil, salt, or hydrogen peroxide unless a veterinarian tells you to. Bring the package to the clinic.

name: Chocolate
toxicCompounds: Theobromine and caffeine
safeServingSize: None. Cats rarely seek chocolate, but a small amount is still a poison exposure.
emergencyAction: Call a poison hotline the same hour. Cats hide illness, so do not wait for dramatic signs.
whatToDoIfIngested: Keep the cat indoors and away from the rest of the chocolate. Do not induce vomiting at home. Note the product and the time.

name: Chocolate
toxicCompounds: Theobromine and caffeine
safeServingSize: None. A bird's small body size means a lick of cocoa can be a serious dose.
emergencyAction: Contact an avian veterinarian or poison hotline immediately and keep the bird warm and quiet.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the food. Do not offer oils or home emetics. Bring the wrapper and the bird to an avian clinic.

name: Chocolate
toxicCompounds: Theobromine and caffeine
safeServingSize: None for rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters, or ferrets.
emergencyAction: Call an exotic-pet veterinarian or poison hotline the same hour.
whatToDoIfIngested: Take the chocolate away. Do not force water or induce vomiting. Note how much is missing.

name: Grapes and raisins
toxicCompounds: Tartaric acid is the leading identified kidney toxin in grapes and raisins
safeServingSize: None. Fresh grapes, raisins, sultanas, and currants are all unsafe. Toxicity is not reliably predicted by the number eaten.
clinicalSymptoms: Little or no urine if the kidneys fail
emergencyAction: Treat any amount as an emergency. Call a poison hotline or clinic before the dog looks sick.
whatToDoIfIngested: Pick up remaining fruit. Do not wait overnight to see if vomiting stops. Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinarian directs it.

name: Grapes and raisins
toxicCompounds: Tartaric acid; kidney injury is proven in dogs and is not a safe experiment in cats
safeServingSize: Do not feed grapes or dried fruit. There is no established safe cat serving.
emergencyAction: Call a veterinarian the same day if a cat eats grapes or raisins.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the fruit, note the amount, and ask the clinic whether to come in. Do not use a home emetic.

name: Xylitol
toxicCompounds: Xylitol (birch-bark sweetener), also listed as birch sugar
safeServingSize: None. Sugar-free gum, peanut butter, baked goods, toothpaste, and some nut butters can contain it. Read the label.
clinicalSymptoms: Weakness or collapse from low blood sugar
Jaundice if the liver is injured
emergencyAction: This is a same-hour emergency. Call poison control with the product label and the dog's weight.
whatToDoIfIngested: Do not offer another sugary food as treatment and do not induce vomiting unless instructed. Rubbing honey on the gums is not a substitute for veterinary care if the dog is collapsing.

name: Xylitol
toxicCompounds: Xylitol; cats do not show the same insulin spike documented in dogs, but the sweetener is still not a cat food
safeServingSize: Do not feed xylitol products. Some liquid medicines use it as a sweetener.
emergencyAction: Call a veterinarian if a cat eats a xylitol product, especially a large amount or a medicine.
whatToDoIfIngested: Save the label. Do not give a second medication to settle the stomach.

name: Onions and garlic
toxicCompounds: Organosulfur compounds in alliums, including N-propyl disulfide
safeServingSize: None. Raw, cooked, powdered, and broth forms all count. Garlic is not a safe flea remedy.
clinicalSymptoms: Red or brown urine from damaged red blood cells
emergencyAction: Call a clinic the same day. Anemia can appear a few days after the meal, so a quiet dog the same evening is not an all-clear.
whatToDoIfIngested: Identify the food, including leftovers, baby food, and seasoned meat. Do not induce vomiting at home.

name: Onions and garlic
toxicCompounds: Allium organosulfur compounds that damage red blood cells
safeServingSize: None. Cats are sensitive, and powdered onion in broth is enough to matter.
emergencyAction: Call a veterinarian the same day and mention onion, garlic, or seasoned table food.
whatToDoIfIngested: Stop the food. Save a sample if you can. Do not wait for pale gums before you call.

name: Onions and garlic
toxicCompounds: Allium organosulfur compounds
safeServingSize: None for rabbits, guinea pigs, hamsters, or ferrets.
emergencyAction: Call an exotic-pet veterinarian the same day.
whatToDoIfIngested: Offer hay or the usual diet only if the animal is still willing to eat. Do not give oils or human antacids.

name: Lilies
toxicCompounds: Unknown water-soluble nephrotoxin in Lilium and Hemerocallis plants
safeServingSize: None. True lilies, including Easter, tiger, Asiatic, and daylilies, can cause kidney failure. Pollen, leaves, flowers, and vase water all count.
emergencyAction: Any chew or pollen exposure is an emergency, even if the cat looks normal. Go to a clinic the same hour.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the plant and wash pollen off the coat with a damp cloth if you can do it without delaying the trip. Do not wait for a urine change.

name: Lilies
toxicCompounds: Plant irritants; true lilies are a kidney emergency in cats and mostly a gastrointestinal irritant in dogs
safeServingSize: Do not let dogs chew lily plants. Peace lilies and calla lilies are different plants and irritate the mouth.
emergencyAction: Call a clinic if a dog eats a large amount or keeps vomiting. If a cat shares the house, treat the plant as a cat emergency.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the plant. Do not induce vomiting unless a veterinarian says to.

name: Avocado
toxicCompounds: Persin, concentrated in the leaves, bark, pit, and fruit of avocado
safeServingSize: None. Guacamole and avocado flesh are not bird treats.
emergencyAction: Contact an avian veterinarian immediately if a bird eats avocado.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the food. Keep the bird warm and quiet. Do not offer oils or home remedies.

name: Avocado
toxicCompounds: Persin is a mild risk in dogs; the pit is a foreign-body and the flesh is high in fat
safeServingSize: Not recommended. A small amount of plain flesh is less dangerous than the pit, skin, or a fatty guacamole.
clinicalSymptoms: Signs of a gut obstruction if the pit was swallowed
emergencyAction: Call a clinic the same day if the pit was eaten or vomiting continues.
whatToDoIfIngested: Do not try to pull a pit from the throat if the dog is choking; go to an emergency hospital. Otherwise save the remaining fruit and call.

name: Macadamia nuts
toxicCompounds: An unidentified toxin in macadamia nuts
safeServingSize: None. Nuts in cookies and trail mix count.
clinicalSymptoms: Weakness, especially in the hind legs
emergencyAction: Call a poison hotline or clinic the same day. Most dogs recover with care, but weakness can look like a spinal emergency.
whatToDoIfIngested: Remove the nuts. Do not give human pain medicine for the weakness. Note how many nuts are missing.

name: Caffeine
toxicCompounds: Caffeine, a methylxanthine like theobromine
safeServingSize: None. Coffee, tea, energy drinks, coffee grounds, and caffeine pills are all sources.
emergencyAction: Call poison control the same hour, especially after grounds, espresso, or a pill.
whatToDoIfIngested: Take the product away. Do not induce vomiting at home. Bring the container.

name: Caffeine
toxicCompounds: Caffeine
safeServingSize: None. A spilled energy drink or coffee grounds can be enough.
emergencyAction: Call a veterinarian or poison hotline the same hour.
whatToDoIfIngested: Keep the cat confined and bring the product label. Do not offer milk as an antidote.

name: Blueberries
toxicCompounds: None identified in plain fresh or frozen blueberries
safeServingSize: A few berries for a small dog, or a small handful for a large dog, as a treat. Treats should stay under about 10 percent of daily calories.
clinicalSymptoms: Loose stool or gas if a large bowl of plain berries is eaten at once
Gagging if a frozen berry is swallowed whole
Vomiting, weakness, or tremors if a sugar-free or baked product was eaten
emergencyAction: Call a clinic if vomiting or diarrhea is severe, or if the berries were in a sweetened or xylitol product.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain blueberries do not need decontamination. Check that the product was not a muffin, jam, or sugar-free snack.

name: Blueberries
toxicCompounds: None identified in a plain berry
safeServingSize: One or two plain berries as an occasional taste. Cats do not need fruit.
clinicalSymptoms: Stomach upset after a large amount
emergencyAction: Call if the cat ate a baked good or a product that might contain xylitol or onion.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain berries can be left alone. Watch appetite and the litter box for a day.

name: Pumpkin
toxicCompounds: None in plain cooked pumpkin. Pumpkin-pie filling adds sugar and spices.
safeServingSize: Plain canned or cooked pumpkin: about 1 teaspoon for a toy dog, up to 1 tablespoon for a large dog, once or twice a day for fiber. Not the pie filling.
clinicalSymptoms: Loose stool or constipation if the portion is too large
emergencyAction: Call if you used pie filling, nutmeg, or xylitol sweetener, or if straining continues.
whatToDoIfIngested: Confirm the can says 100 percent pumpkin. Offer water. A veterinarian should guide long-term use for diarrhea.

name: Pumpkin
toxicCompounds: None in plain cooked pumpkin
safeServingSize: About 1 teaspoon of plain pumpkin mixed into food. It is a fiber aid, not a meal.
clinicalSymptoms: A skipped meal if the cat dislikes the texture
Loose stool from too much fiber
emergencyAction: Call the same day if a cat stops eating, strains in the box, or ate pie filling.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain pumpkin does not need emergency care. Do not force a cat who refuses it.

name: Plain cooked chicken
toxicCompounds: None in unseasoned cooked meat. Bones splinter, and onion or garlic seasoning is toxic.
safeServingSize: Boneless, skinless, unseasoned cooked chicken as a topper or a short bland meal. It is not a complete diet.
clinicalSymptoms: Pancreatitis signs after fatty skin or a large greasy portion
Choking or vomiting if bones were eaten
emergencyAction: Go to a clinic for bone choking, repeated vomiting, or a painful abdomen.
whatToDoIfIngested: Skip treats if the meat was plain and boneless. Call if it was cooked with alliums or if bones were swallowed.

name: Plain cooked chicken
toxicCompounds: None in plain cooked meat. Seasoning and bones are the hazards.
safeServingSize: Small pieces of boneless, unseasoned cooked chicken. A chicken-only diet lacks calcium and taurine balance over time.
clinicalSymptoms: Constipation or urinary changes are separate problems and still need a check
emergencyAction: Call the same day if a male cat strains in the litter box, or if bones were eaten.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain chicken can stay down. Remove any seasoned leftovers.

name: Carrots
toxicCompounds: None in plain raw or cooked carrot
safeServingSize: A few raw sticks or cooked coins as a low-calorie treat. Cut rounds for dogs who gulp food.
clinicalSymptoms: Loose stool after a large amount
Choking on a large uncut piece
emergencyAction: Seek care for choking or if vomiting continues.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain carrot does not need treatment. Supervise crunchy pieces.

name: Carrots
toxicCompounds: None. Carrot is a sugary treat for rabbits and guinea pigs, not a hay replacement.
safeServingSize: A thin slice a few times a week for a rabbit or guinea pig. Unlimited timothy hay remains the main food.
clinicalSymptoms: Soft droppings if sugary treats replace hay
Reduced appetite if the gut slows
emergencyAction: Call an exotic veterinarian the same day if droppings stop or the animal hunches and grinds its teeth.
whatToDoIfIngested: Return to hay. A single carrot slice does not need emergency care.

name: Green beans
toxicCompounds: None in plain fresh, frozen, or canned beans with no salt
safeServingSize: A small handful of plain cut beans. Skip salted canned beans and bean casseroles.
clinicalSymptoms: Gas or loose stool from a large portion
emergencyAction: Call if the beans were cooked with onion, garlic, or a sugar-free sauce.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain beans can be left alone. Offer water.

name: Salmon
toxicCompounds: None in fully cooked salmon. Raw Pacific salmon can carry the Neorickettsia helminthoeca fluke in some regions.
safeServingSize: A small portion of boneless, fully cooked salmon without seasoning. Remove skin if it is very fatty. Do not feed raw salmon.
clinicalSymptoms: Fever, vomiting, and enlarged nodes days after raw salmon in endemic areas
emergencyAction: Call a clinic if the salmon was raw, still had bones, or the dog becomes weak or feverish.
whatToDoIfIngested: Cooked boneless salmon does not need decontamination. Save details if it was raw or smoked with seasoning.

name: Salmon
toxicCompounds: None in plain cooked salmon. Raw fish is an incomplete diet and can carry parasites.
safeServingSize: A teaspoon or two of boneless cooked salmon as a topper, not a daily diet. Bones and onion seasoning are unsafe.
emergencyAction: Call if bones were eaten or the fish was packed in onion sauce.
whatToDoIfIngested: Plain cooked salmon can stay in the meal plan for that day. Remove skin and bones next time.

name: Timothy hay
toxicCompounds: None. Dusty or moldy hay is the hazard, not the grass itself.
safeServingSize: Unlimited fresh timothy hay for adult rabbits and guinea pigs. Alfalfa hay is for growing or nursing animals, not the default adult diet.
clinicalSymptoms: No droppings and hunching if the animal stops eating hay
emergencyAction: A rabbit or guinea pig that stops eating hay needs a same-day exotic veterinarian. Gut stasis is an emergency.
whatToDoIfIngested: Keep hay available. Throw out wet or moldy flakes. Do not replace hay with pellets or carrots.
